topic: AWS Amplify for AI interfaces

AWS Amplify with AI kit components that abstract FM streaming and conversation management

AWS Glue DataBrew

topic: CloudWatch Logs Insights for FM debugging
question_text: A developer needs to analyse the prompts and responses that led to a spike in poor-quality FM outputs over the past 24 hours. Which tool should they use?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to query structured log records of prompts and responses
Amazon Inspector to scan logs for vulnerabilities
AWS Config to review resource changes during the spike
Amazon Athena to query S3 access logs

explanation: Skill 2.5.6 explicitly cites CloudWatch Logs Insights for analysing prompts and responses to improve troubleshooting efficiency. With Bedrock Model Invocation Logging enabled, prompts and responses are logged to CloudWatch Logs, enabling Logs Insights queries to filter by time window, response quality signals, and error codes. Athena queries S3 files — useful if logs are archived to S3, but CloudWatch Logs Insights is the real-time first step.

topic: No-code prompt workflow builder
question_text: A business analyst without coding experience wants to build a multi-step GenAI workflow that chains several FM calls together to process customer feedback. Which Bedrock feature supports this without writing code?

AWS Step Functions Express Workflows

topic: OpenAPI-first GenAI integration
question_text: A company is building a new GenAI-powered API and wants its interface contract defined before any implementation begins, ensuring all consumers have a consistent expectation. Which approach supports this?

options.text: Implement the API first, then generate documentation from the code
Define the API contract first with an OpenAPI (Swagger) specification, then import it into API Gateway and implement Lambda handlers
Share the Lambda function ARN directly with consumers
Use Amazon EventBridge schema registry as the primary API contract

explanation: Skill 2.5.2 cites OpenAPI specifications for API-first development approaches. Defining the OpenAPI spec first allows consumers to generate client SDKs, write integration tests, and develop in parallel — before any backend implementation exists. API Gateway can import the OpenAPI spec directly to create routes, validation, and documentation. Code-first documentation risks inconsistency. Sharing Lambda ARNs is an internal implementation detail, not a consumer-facing contract. EventBridge schema registry is for event schemas, not request/response API contracts.
source_topic: OpenAPI specification, API-first development, API Gateway

topic: Q Business vs Bedrock Knowledge Bases
question_text: A company wants internal staff (HR, Sales, Finance) to search company documents using natural-language queries, with the search results strictly limited by each user's existing SharePoint permissions. They need minimal development effort and no custom UI code. Which solution is most appropriate?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with a custom Lambda access-control layer
Amazon Q Business — managed enterprise RAG with built-in ACL inheritance from connected data sources
Amazon Kendra with a custom post-processing Lambda for access control
Build a custom RAG application using LangChain and Bedrock

explanation: Amazon Q Business (Skill 2.5.2, accessible AI interfaces) is a fully managed enterprise RAG service that inherits access control lists (ACL) directly from connected data sources like SharePoint — users only see documents they already have permission to access, enforced automatically. It provides a built-in web experience with no custom UI code needed. Bedrock Knowledge Bases (A) provides flexible RAG but requires building a custom access-control layer. Kendra (C) is being closed to new customers (July 2026). Custom LangChain (D) maximises flexibility but is the highest-effort option — opposite of minimal development.
source_topic: Amazon Q Business, ACL, managed enterprise RAG

topic: Q Business Plugins for write actions
question_text: A company uses Amazon Q Business for internal employee support. Employees want to not just find answers but also create Jira tickets directly from the chat interface without leaving Q Business. Which Q Business feature enables write actions to external systems?

options.text: Q Business Data Connectors — extend them to write back to Jira
Q Business Plugins — pre-built enterprise connectors (Jira, ServiceNow, Salesforce) that enable write actions
Amazon Bedrock Agents action groups connected to Q Business
Q Business cannot take write actions — it is read-only

explanation: Q Business Plugins are pre-built enterprise connectors (Jira, ServiceNow, Salesforce, Zendesk) that enable write actions directly from the chat interface. Data Connectors (A) are read-only ingestion connectors — they index documents but cannot write back to source systems. Bedrock Agents action groups are a different product not embedded in Q Business. Q Business supports write actions via Plugins — it is not read-only.
source_topic: Amazon Q Business Plugins, enterprise write actions

topic: SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking for audit
question_text: A regulated financial services firm needs to audit their ML pipeline to trace which training dataset version produced a given deployed model endpoint. Which SageMaker capability provides this end-to-end lineage tracking?

options.text: SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking — automatically tracks relationships between datasets, training jobs, models, and endpoints; queryable via the LineageQuery API
SageMaker Model Monitor — detects data drift in production traffic
SageMaker Clarify — explains model predictions with SHAP values
SageMaker Ground Truth — labels training data

explanation: SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking creates and stores a graph of ML workflow entities (datasets, training jobs, models, endpoints) and their associations. The LineageQuery API lets you trace forward and backward through this graph — e.g. find all endpoints using a specific dataset. Model Monitor detects data drift, Clarify explains predictions, and Ground Truth labels data; none of these provide lineage tracking.
source_topic: SageMaker Lineage Tracking, ML audit, LineageQuery API

topic: SageMaker Ground Truth — training data labeling
question_text: A company is building a custom image classification model and needs to label 50,000 images efficiently. They want a managed AWS service that combines automated pre-labeling with a human review workflow. Which service is purpose-built for this?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth — provides automated labeling and a managed workforce (Mechanical Turk, private, or vendor) for human review
Amazon Rekognition — automatically labels images without human review
Amazon Textract — extracts text from images
Amazon A2I — routes already-labeled data for human review only

explanation: SageMaker Ground Truth is AWS's managed data labeling service. It uses automated pre-labeling to label high-confidence examples and routes uncertain examples to a human workforce (Amazon Mechanical Turk, private team, or AWS-managed vendors). Rekognition performs inference but does not build training datasets through human labeling pipelines. Textract extracts text. A2I is for augmenting model predictions with human review — not for building initial training label sets.
source_topic: SageMaker Ground Truth, training data labeling, HITL

topic: SageMaker Feature Store

Amazon DynamoDB — a NoSQL database with no ML-specific feature management
Amazon Redshift — a data warehouse for analytical SQL queries only
Amazon ElastiCache — an in-memory cache for general application data

explanation: SageMaker Feature Store is purpose-built for ML feature management. It has an online store (low-latency reads for real-time inference) and an offline store (S3-backed for batch training access) in a single managed service, with feature group versioning. DynamoDB is a general NoSQL database with no feature lineage or dual-store design. Redshift is an analytical warehouse. ElastiCache is a general-purpose cache.
source_topic: SageMaker Feature Store, online/offline store, feature engineering

Bedrock Prompt Flows with Lambda integration

topic: Clarify vs Model Monitor distinction
question_text: A company has two requirements: (1) detect and explain bias in their training data BEFORE model deployment, and (2) detect data drift and performance degradation AFTER model deployment. Which combination of SageMaker services addresses BOTH requirements?

options.text: SageMaker Clarify (for both pre- and post-deployment)
SageMaker Model Monitor (for both)
SageMaker Clarify (pre-deployment bias/explainability) + SageMaker Model Monitor (post-deployment drift detection)
SageMaker Ground Truth (bias detection) + SageMaker Pipelines (drift detection)

explanation: SageMaker Clarify detects bias in training data and provides SHAP-based explainability for model predictions — primarily a pre-deployment and offline analysis tool. SageMaker Model Monitor continuously monitors live endpoints for data drift, concept drift, and performance degradation post-deployment. Together they cover the full pre/post lifecycle. Clarify alone doesn't continuously monitor live traffic. Model Monitor alone doesn't do pre-training bias analysis.
source_topic: SageMaker Clarify + Model Monitor for full bias/drift lifecycle

topic: SageMaker Feature Store
question_text: A fintech company trains multiple fraud detection models using the same features (30-day transaction count, velocity, account age). Different teams independently re-compute these features, causing inconsistencies between training and inference. What AWS service resolves this?

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB — store features per model
Amazon SageMaker Feature Store — centralised online/offline feature repository
AWS Glue Data Catalog — catalogue all feature tables
Amazon S3 — store feature CSVs per team

explanation: SageMaker Feature Store is the purpose-built solution for this problem: it provides a single source of truth for ML features with both an online store (low-latency, real-time inference) and offline store (batch training). All teams read from the same definitions, eliminating training-serving skew. DynamoDB lacks feature-specific semantics. Glue Data Catalog is metadata, not a feature runtime. S3 CSVs per-team causes the exact duplication/inconsistency problem.
source_topic: SageMaker Feature Store eliminating training-serving skew

topic: Glue DataBrew for visual data preparation
question_text: A business analyst (non-coder) needs to profile a CSV dataset for missing values, outliers, and distributions, then apply 20 transformations (normalization, encoding, date parsing) and save the recipe for reuse on future datasets. Which AWS service is MOST appropriate?

options.text: AWS Glue ETL (PySpark jobs)
Amazon SageMaker Processing jobs
AWS Glue DataBrew (visual, no-code data preparation)
Amazon Athena SQL queries

explanation: AWS Glue DataBrew provides a visual, no-code interface with 250+ built-in transformations, interactive data profiling (missing values, distributions, outliers), and reusable Recipes that can be applied to new datasets. It requires no coding, making it ideal for business analysts. Glue ETL requires PySpark code. SageMaker Processing requires Python scripts. Athena is SQL-based querying, not a visual transformation tool.
source_topic: Glue DataBrew no-code visual data preparation with Recipes

topic: Continued Pre-Training vs fine-tuning
question_text: A pharmaceutical company wants to adapt a Bedrock foundation model to deeply understand proprietary drug discovery research papers. The papers are NOT annotated with labels. Which customisation technique is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Instruction-based fine-tuning on labelled Q&A pairs from the papers
Continued Pre-Training (CPT) on the unlabelled domain-specific research papers
Prompt engineering with few-shot examples from papers
RAG using the papers as a knowledge base

explanation: Continued Pre-Training (CPT) adapts a foundation model using unlabelled domain-specific data — exactly what is available here (research papers without annotations). This extends the model's domain knowledge without requiring labelled examples. Instruction-based fine-tuning requires labelled prompt-response pairs. Prompt engineering doesn't modify model weights. RAG retrieves at inference time but doesn't build deep domain knowledge into the model itself.
source_topic: Continued Pre-Training vs instruction fine-tuning

topic: Instruction-based vs domain-adaptation fine-tuning
question_text: A company wants to fine-tune a Bedrock model to follow a specific multi-step conversational format for handling customer support tickets — responding with Acknowledge, Diagnose, Suggest, Confirm steps. They have 2,000 labelled example conversations. Which fine-tuning approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Continued Pre-Training on unlabelled conversation logs
Domain adaptation fine-tuning on customer support terminology
Instruction-based fine-tuning on labelled prompt-response pairs demonstrating the required format
LoRA fine-tuning on a general-purpose dataset

explanation: Instruction-based fine-tuning is designed for teaching a model to follow specific instructions, tasks, or conversational formats using labelled prompt-response examples. With 2,000 labelled examples of the required multi-step format, this is the correct approach. Continued Pre-Training uses unlabelled data to extend domain knowledge. Domain adaptation fine-tuning adapts to specialised vocabulary, not structured behavioural formats. LoRA is a PEFT technique (how to fine-tune efficiently), not a fine-tuning objective type.
source_topic: Instruction-based fine-tuning for task-specific behaviour

Amazon Q Apps (within Amazon Q Business)

Amazon Connect Q in Connect

topic: CloudWatch Logs Insights for FM debugging
question_text: A team logs all Bedrock prompt and response pairs to CloudWatch Logs. They want to query the logs to find all invocations where the response contained the phrase 'I cannot help with that' in the last 24 hours. Which tool enables this analysis?

options.text: AWS CloudTrail — query API management events
Amazon Athena — query S3 log files
CloudWatch Logs Insights — interactive query language on CloudWatch log data
Amazon OpenSearch — full-text search on indexed logs

explanation: CloudWatch Logs Insights provides an interactive SQL-like query language for analysing CloudWatch log data in real time. A query like `fields @timestamp, @message | filter @message like /I cannot help with that/ | sort @timestamp desc` would find all matching log events. CloudTrail records management API calls, not prompt/response content. Athena queries data in S3, not CloudWatch Logs directly. OpenSearch is a separate service requiring log streaming setup.
source_topic: CloudWatch Logs Insights for Bedrock response pattern analysis

topic: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store vs AppConfig
question_text: A developer is choosing between AWS services for three different configuration needs: (1) storing a third-party API key with auto-rotation, (2) storing the active Bedrock model ID that changes occasionally at runtime, (3) storing environment-specific Lambda environment variables. Which BEST mapping of service to use case is correct?

options.text: All three: AWS Secrets Manager
API key → Secrets Manager; model ID → AppConfig; env variables → Parameter Store (SecureString)
API key → AppConfig; model ID → Secrets Manager; env variables → Parameter Store
All three: Parameter Store

explanation: Secrets Manager is purpose-built for sensitive credentials (API keys) with automatic rotation. AppConfig is designed for feature flags and runtime configuration values (like active model IDs) that change dynamically without redeployment. Parameter Store (SecureString) is appropriate for environment-specific configuration values like Lambda env vars. Using Secrets Manager for all three is unnecessarily expensive. AppConfig for API keys (C) is wrong — it has no rotation support.
source_topic: Secrets Manager vs AppConfig vs Parameter Store decision
